title: Node.js Streams: A Handwritten Field Guide
summary: A dense, example-driven handbook on Node.js streams — the four stream types, object mode, the internal buffering and backpressure machinery, pipe vs pipeline, async iteration, and the error-handling and leak traps that bite in production. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet of rules and comparisons.

chapters.title: Why Streams Exist
points: Definition: a stream is an abstraction for data that arrives or is consumed over time, in chunks, instead of all at once.
The problem streams solve: `fs.readFileSync('10gb.log')` loads 10 GB into RSS; a read stream holds only ~64 KB at a time.
Memory profile comparison: buffered read = O(file size) memory; streamed read = O(highWaterMark) memory, independent of file size.
Latency win: time-to-first-byte is O(1) with streams vs O(n) buffered — an HTTP proxy can start writing to the client before the origin finishes.
Composability: streams are Unix pipes in JS — `read | transform | transform | write` builds pipelines from small single-purpose parts.
Streams are EventEmitters: every stream inherits `on`, `emit`, `once`, so the API is event-driven, not promise-driven by default.

Where streams already are in Node core: `fs.createReadStream`, `http.IncomingMessage` (readable), `http.ServerResponse` (writable), `zlib.createGzip` (transform), `crypto.createHash` (writable/transform), `net.Socket` (duplex), `process.stdin`/`stdout`.
Chunks are `Buffer` by default; strings if an encoding is set; arbitrary JS values in object mode.
Example that motivates the whole handbook: `fs.createReadStream('in.txt').pipe(zlib.createGzip()).pipe(fs.createWriteStream('out.gz'))` — constant memory regardless of input size.
Mental model to carry through: producer → bounded buffer → consumer, with a feedback signal running backwards.

chapters.title: The Four Stream Types
points: Readable: a source you read from. Emits `data`/`readable`/`end`. Examples: `fs.createReadStream`, HTTP request on the server.
Writable: a sink you write to. Has `write()`/`end()`, emits `drain`/`finish`. Examples: `fs.createWriteStream`, HTTP response on the server.
Duplex: independent readable and writable sides in one object, with no required relationship between them. Example: `net.Socket` — what you write goes to the peer, what you read came from the peer.
Transform: a Duplex where the readable side is a function of the written side. Example: `zlib.createGzip()`, `crypto.createCipheriv()`.
PassThrough: a Transform that outputs its input unchanged — used as a tee point, a placeholder, or a buffer to observe bytes flowing by.
Class hierarchy: `Stream` → `Readable`/`Writable`; `Duplex extends Readable` and mixes in `Writable`; `Transform extends Duplex`; `PassThrough extends Transform`.
Which side do you implement? Readable → `_read(size)`; Writable → `_write(chunk, enc, cb)`; Transform → `_transform(chunk, enc, cb)` and optionally `_flush(cb)`.
Underscore methods are the internal contract — you implement them, you never call them. The public API (`read`, `write`, `push`) calls them for you.
Duplex vs Transform decision rule: if the output is derived from the input, use Transform; if the two sides are unrelated channels, use Duplex.
Every stream type supports object mode via `{ objectMode: true }` in the constructor options.

chapters.title: Readable Streams: Two Modes
points: Every readable starts paused; it enters flowing mode when you attach a `data` handler, call `.resume()`, or `.pipe()` somewhere.
Flowing mode: chunks are pushed at you via `stream.on('data', chunk => ...)` as fast as the source produces them.
Paused mode: you pull with `stream.on('readable', () => { let c; while ((c = stream.read()) !== null) ... })`.
`.pause()` and `.resume()` switch modes; removing all `data` listeners does NOT automatically re-pause (the mode stays flowing).
Danger: attaching a `data` listener without a destination discards backpressure entirely — you are draining the source into memory or into nothing.
`readable.read(n)` returns `n` bytes, or `null` if fewer than `n` are buffered; `read()` with no arg returns everything buffered.
Events in lifecycle order: `readable` → `data` → `end` (source exhausted) → `close` (resources released). `end` never fires if you never consume.
`setEncoding('utf8')` makes chunks strings and correctly handles multi-byte characters split across chunk boundaries — a manual `chunk.toString()` per chunk does not.
Async iteration is the modern default: `for await (const chunk of readable) { ... }` — respects backpressure and propagates errors as exceptions.
Helpers: `Readable.from(iterable)` builds a readable from any (async) iterable; `stream.toArray()` and `stream.toWeb()` exist on modern Node.

chapters.title: Implementing a Readable
points: Contract: implement `_read(size)`; inside it, call `this.push(chunk)` one or more times to supply data.
`push()` returns `false` when the internal buffer has exceeded `highWaterMark` — a hint to stop pushing until `_read` is called again.
`this.push(null)` signals end-of-stream (EOF). Forgetting it means the consumer's `end` event never fires and the pipeline hangs.
`_read` is never called re-entrantly: Node calls it again only after you push at least once (or after `read()` drains the buffer).
Minimal counter example: `new Readable({ read() { this.push(this.i < 5 ? String(this.i++) : null) } })`.
Async source: `_read(size) { fetchNext().then(v => this.push(v)).catch(e => this.destroy(e)) }` — never throw synchronously out of `_read`.
Object mode: `new Readable({ objectMode: true })` lets you push objects; `highWaterMark` then counts objects (default 16), not bytes.
`Readable.from(asyncGenerator())` replaces most hand-written `_read` implementations — prefer it unless you need fine control.
Report errors with `this.destroy(err)`, which emits `error` then `close`; do not `emit('error')` directly.
Gotcha: pushing in a tight loop without checking `push()`'s return value defeats the highWaterMark and grows the buffer without bound.

chapters.title: Writable Streams and the drain Event
points: `writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean: `true` = keep writing, `false` = internal buffer is at or over `highWaterMark`, stop and wait.
The return value is advisory, not enforced — writes after `false` are still accepted and still buffered, which is exactly how memory blows up.
The correct pause/resume protocol: when `write()` returns `false`, stop; resume only after the `drain` event fires.
Canonical loop: `function push() { while (i < n && stream.write(data[i++])); if (i < n) stream.once('drain', push); }`.
`end([chunk])` finishes the stream; further `write()` calls emit an `ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END` error.
`finish` fires when `end()` was called and all buffered data has been flushed to the underlying resource.
`close` fires when the underlying resource is released; `finish` does not imply the file descriptor is closed.
`cork()`/`uncork()` batch small writes into fewer underlying syscalls; always pair them, and uncork on the next tick.
Implementing one: `_write(chunk, encoding, callback)` — call `callback()` exactly once when the chunk is handled, `callback(err)` on failure. Calling it twice throws.
`_writev(chunks, cb)` is the optional batched variant, used when writes are corked or queued.
`_final(cb)` runs once before `finish` — the place to flush trailers or close handles.
Gotcha: never call `callback()` synchronously in a hot path from `_write` without care — it can starve the event loop; `process.nextTick(callback)` is the usual fix.

chapters.title: Backpressure: The Core Idea
points: Definition: backpressure is the feedback signal a slow consumer sends to a fast producer telling it to slow down.
Without it: producer at 100 MB/s, consumer at 10 MB/s, the 90 MB/s difference accumulates in process memory until OOM.
The buffer is bounded by `highWaterMark` — default 64 KB (65536) for byte streams, 16 for object-mode streams.
highWaterMark is a threshold, not a hard cap: Node buffers past it, it only flips the signal from `true` to `false`.
The writable signal: `write()` returning `false`, cleared by `drain`.
The readable signal: `push()` returning `false`, cleared by the next `_read()` call.
How pipe wires them together: on `write() === false`, pipe calls `src.pause()`; on `drain`, it calls `src.resume()`.
In a 3-stage pipeline the signal propagates backwards stage by stage — the sink stalls the transform, which stalls the source.
Tuning: a bigger highWaterMark means more throughput and fewer mode switches at the cost of memory; a smaller one means lower latency and memory.
Diagnosing a leak: rising `writableLength` / `readableLength` over time means one side is ignoring the signal.
Rule of thumb: if you are not using `pipe`, `pipeline`, or `for await`, you are responsible for backpressure by hand — and probably getting it wrong.

chapters.title: Transform Streams
points: A Transform sits mid-pipeline: written chunks go in the writable side, `push()`ed chunks come out the readable side.
Implement `_transform(chunk, encoding, callback)`; push zero, one, or many chunks per input chunk, then call `callback()`.
One-to-one example — uppercase: `_transform(c, e, cb) { this.push(c.toString().toUpperCase()); cb(); }`.
One-to-many example — a line splitter buffers a partial line, pushes each complete line, and keeps the remainder for the next chunk.
Many-to-one example — batching: accumulate N objects, push the array only when full.
`_flush(callback)` runs after the last chunk and before `end` — the only place to emit a trailing partial line or a final batch. Forgetting it silently drops the tail.
`callback(err)` (or `callback(null, chunk)` as a shorthand push) is how a transform reports failure and stops the pipeline.
Async transform: `async _transform(c, e, cb) { try { cb(null, await work(c)) } catch (err) { cb(err) } }` — a rejected promise is not auto-caught.
Object mode transforms are the workhorse of ETL: `objectMode: true` on both sides lets you pipe rows, records, or JSON values.
Chunk boundaries are arbitrary: a transform must never assume one input chunk equals one logical record. This is the #1 transform bug.
Core transforms to know: `zlib.createGzip/Gunzip`, `crypto.createCipheriv`, `stream.PassThrough`.

chapters.title: pipe() vs pipeline()
points: `src.pipe(dest)` wires data and backpressure and returns `dest`, so it chains: `a.pipe(b).pipe(c)`.
Fatal flaw of `pipe`: it does NOT forward errors. An error on `a` leaves `b` and `c` open and un-destroyed — a file descriptor and memory leak.
`pipe` also does not auto-destroy on error, so a failed pipeline can leave sockets hanging until timeout.
The workaround people write — `.on('error', ...)` on every stage plus manual `destroy()` — is exactly what `pipeline` does for you.
`stream.pipeline(a, b, c, cb)` pipes all stages, forwards errors to the single callback, and destroys every stream on failure or completion.
Promise form: `const { pipeline } = require('node:stream/promises'); await pipeline(a, b, c)` — errors become a rejection.
`pipeline` accepts async generators as stages: `pipeline(src, async function* (source) { for await (const c of source) yield transform(c) }, dest)`.
Cancellation: pass `{ signal: abortController.signal }` to abort a pipeline mid-flight; it rejects with `AbortError`.
`stream.finished(stream, cb)` (and its promise form) detects end/error/close on a single stream without piping.
Comparison row — error handling: `pipe` = manual per stage; `pipeline` = centralized. Cleanup: `pipe` = none; `pipeline` = automatic destroy. Return: `pipe` = dest; `pipeline` = callback or promise.
Rule: use `pipeline` in all application code. Reach for raw `pipe` only in a one-liner script where a crash is acceptable.

chapters.title: Error Handling
points: Streams are EventEmitters: an unhandled `error` event throws and crashes the process. There is no default handler.
`destroy(err)` is the correct way to fail a stream: it emits `error`, then `close`, and prevents further I/O.
After `destroy()`, `writable.destroyed` and `readable.destroyed` are `true`; writes are rejected.
`autoDestroy` defaults to `true` on modern Node, so streams destroy themselves after `end`/`finish`.
Errors do not propagate through `pipe` in either direction — each stage needs its own listener if you insist on using `pipe`.
With `pipeline`, one handler catches an error from any stage, and the error object tells you which stage failed.
Common runtime errors to recognize: `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` (a stage closed before `end`), `ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END`, `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED`, `EPIPE` (peer went away).
Cleanup rule: an error on any stage must destroy the others, or you leak file descriptors — the `EMFILE: too many open files` crash traced back to leaked pipes.
In `_transform`/`_write`, report errors via `callback(err)`; do not `throw` from an async callback, where nothing will catch it.
`for await` converts stream errors into `try/catch`-able exceptions, but breaking out of the loop early destroys the stream — usually what you want, occasionally a surprise.
HTTP-specific trap: if the response has already begun streaming, headers are sent, so you cannot switch to a 500 — you can only destroy the socket.

chapters.title: Object Mode and Async Iteration
points: `{ objectMode: true }` lets chunks be any JS value except `null` (`null` still means EOF).
In object mode `highWaterMark` counts items, defaulting to 16 — a huge behavioral difference from the 64 KB byte default.
`readableObjectMode` and `writableObjectMode` can be set independently — key for a parser that takes Buffers in and emits objects out.
Classic pipeline shape: file → line splitter (bytes → strings) → JSON parser (strings → objects) → DB writer (objects → side effects).
`for await (const row of stream)` gives backpressure for free: the loop body's await time throttles the source.
An async generator is a Transform in disguise, and is legal as a `pipeline` stage — often more readable than a Transform subclass.
`Readable.from(asyncGen())` adapts any async iterable (a paginated API, a DB cursor) into a stream.
Modern iterator helpers on Readable: `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`, `.reduce()`, `.toArray()`, with a `{ concurrency }` option on map/filter.
Trade-off: object mode costs more per chunk (no batched Buffers) but makes record-oriented code far simpler; for raw bytes stay out of object mode.
Gotcha: pushing `null` in object mode to represent a legitimate null value ends the stream. Wrap it, or use a sentinel.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Ignoring `write()`'s return value — memory grows without bound under load. The bug only shows up in production, at scale.
Using `pipe` without per-stage error handlers — a source error leaves the destination open forever.
Assuming chunk boundaries align with logical records — a JSON object or a UTF-8 character split across two chunks corrupts the parse. Fix: buffer the remainder, or use `setEncoding`.
Forgetting `push(null)` in `_read` or a missing `_flush` — the consumer hangs waiting for an `end` that never comes.
Calling the `_write`/`_transform` callback twice — throws `ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK`.
Mixing paused and flowing mode: attaching a `data` handler and also calling `read()` produces missing chunks.
Attaching `data` early to "peek", then piping later — the first chunks are already gone. Use `PassThrough` or `pause()` first.
`finish` ≠ file on disk. Wait for `close` (or `fsync`) before telling the user the upload is durable.
Building a whole array of chunks and concatenating at the end — that is just a buffered read with extra steps; you gave up the only benefit of streaming.
Not handling client disconnects: on `req.aborted`/`close`, destroy the upstream source or it keeps reading into nowhere.
Setting a huge `highWaterMark` to "fix" slowness — it hides backpressure rather than fixing the slow consumer.
Awaiting inside a `data` handler — the handler is not awaited, so chunks keep arriving and concurrency is unbounded. Use `for await` instead.

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet and Summary
points: Type table — Readable: `_read`/`push`/`end` event. Writable: `_write`/`write`/`drain`+`finish`. Duplex: both, unrelated. Transform: `_transform`+`_flush`, output derived from input.
Backpressure signals in one line: `write() === false` → wait for `drain`; `push() === false` → stop until `_read`.
Defaults to memorize: byte highWaterMark 64 KB, object-mode highWaterMark 16, `autoDestroy: true`, `emitClose: true`.
Event order, readable: `readable` → `data` → `end` → `close`. Writable: `drain` (repeatable) → `finish` → `close`. Error at any point → `error` → `close`.
Memory complexity: buffered = O(n) in input size; streamed = O(highWaterMark) — constant regardless of input.
API choice: `pipeline` (promise form) for production, `for await` for per-record logic, raw `pipe` only for throwaway scripts.
Error rule: one `pipeline` callback beats N `pipe` error listeners; always `destroy(err)`, never `emit('error')`.
Implementation checklist: push `null` at EOF, implement `_flush` if you buffer, call the callback exactly once, never assume chunk boundaries.
When NOT to stream: small files, data you need fully in memory anyway (sorting, JSON.parse of a whole document), or when a simple `readFile` is clearer.
Alternatives worth knowing: Web Streams (`ReadableStream`/`WritableStream`) interoperate via `Readable.toWeb`/`fromWeb`; async iterators cover many cases without any stream class at all.
Final rule: streams are a memory-bounded pipe with a backwards feedback wire. If you break the wire, you break the memory bound.
